{{nihongo|'''Shiramine Shrine'''|白峯神宮|Shiramine jingū}} is a Shinto Shrine in {{ill|Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto|en|Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto|qid=Q1321824|lt=Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto}}<ref name="kanpei-taisha1940">Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 126.</ref>

The Shrine is dedicated to the veneration of the ''kami'' of {{ill|Emperor Junnin|en|Emperor Junnin|qid=Q329713|lt=Emperor Junnin}}<ref name="kanpei-taisha1940"/> and {{ill|Emperor Sutoku|en|Emperor Sutoku|qid=Q349287|lt=Emperor Sutoku}}. Annually in mid–September two Noh performances are held at the Shiramine Shrine in memory of Emperor Sutoku.<ref>Kerr, Amy. [http://www.artflock.com/blog/post/toyokuni-jinja-annual-festival-noh-plays-at-shiramine-shrine-toaji-temple-special-opening-markets-japan-post-day/  "Noh Plays at Shiramine Shrine."] September 2008.</ref>

Shiramine is also home to the deity Seidai Myojin who is popularly known as the god of sports, and especially soccer.<ref>[https://www.reuters.com/article/lifestyleMolt/idUSSP30406620070717  "Japan shrine keeps ancient soccer alive and kicking,"] Reuters. July 17, 2007.</ref>

[[File:Shiramine Shrine.JPG|thumb|Shrine exterior]]

The lucky charm(叶う輪 Kanauwa) of Shiramine Shrine is very popular to worshipers. Kanauwa is Lucky charm of sports.
[[File:叶う輪 主なタイプ.jpg|thumb|Kanauwa is Lucky charm of sports.]]
[[File:小町踊り.jpg|thumb|Komachi-odori]]

==Kanpei-sha==
In 1871, the {{nihongo|''Kanpei-sha''|官幣社}} identified the hierarchy of government-supported shrines most closely associated with the Imperial family.<ref name="imperial124">Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 124.</ref>  The ''kampeisha'' were shrines venerated by the imperial family.  This Category encompasses those sanctuaries enshrining emperors, imperial family members, or meritorious retainers of the Imperial family.<ref name="system">Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics, Kokugakuin University: [http://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_K.html  Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms, ''Kampei Taisha.'']</ref>  Up through 1940, the mid-range of Imperial shrines or {{nihongo|''[[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-chūsha]]''|官幣中社}} included  the shrine; and it was then known as Shiramine''-gū''<ref name="imperial125">Ponsonby-Fane. ''Imperial,'' p. 125.</ref> In 1940, Shiramine's status was changed to {{nihongo|''Kanpei-taisha''|官幣大社}}, which is the highest Rank; and since then, it has been known as Shiramine ''jingū.''<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1963). ''The Vicissitudes of Shinto,'' p. 394.</ref>
